title: Vectors: The Dot Product, the Cross Product, and Cross Track Error

questions.question: Why is a distance from the path not enough to steer a robot back onto it?
options: It does not say which side the robot is on, and turning either way reduces a distance
Distances are too slow to compute
Because the path may be curved
Because distance is always positive in floating point
questions.explanation: The controller needs a signed quantity. That sign is what the cross product supplies, and it is why cross track error is signed rather than a magnitude.

questions.question: What does the sign of the dot product tell you?
options: Whether the two directions broadly agree, so whether a target is ahead or behind
Which side of the path the robot is on
How far apart the vectors are
Whether the vectors are the same length
questions.explanation: Positive means they point the same way, negative means opposed. That single test answers is this in front of me, which is worth the whole operation.

questions.question: What does the two dimensional cross product give you?
options: One signed number: zero when parallel, positive when the second is turned anticlockwise
A third vector perpendicular to both
The distance between the vectors
The angle in degrees
questions.explanation: In two dimensions it collapses to a single number, the signed area of the parallelogram the vectors span, and its sign answers which way.

questions.question: Why compute an angle with atan2 of the cross and the dot rather than acos?
options: acos loses small angles entirely, can leave its domain and return NaN, and has no sign
atan2 is faster
acos only works on unit vectors
atan2 returns degrees, which is more useful
questions.explanation: Measured on a real machine, acos returns exactly zero for a true angle of 1e-8. atan2 returns it correctly, is well conditioned everywhere, and answers a signed angle already in range.

questions.question: Why divide the cross product by the length of the path segment?
options: The cross product is an area, and dividing by the base turns it into a height
To normalise the sign
To convert radians to metres
Because the cross product is otherwise too large to store
questions.explanation: The perpendicular distance is the height of the parallelogram. The sign survives the division, which is what keeps the answer signed.

questions.question: What should normalising a zero vector return?
options: The zero vector, decided deliberately, because there is no direction to give
A vector of length one pointing along x
NaN, which correctly signals the problem
It should throw an exception
questions.explanation: Dividing by a length of zero fills the result with NaN, which spreads silently through everything downstream. Answering deliberately is what stops that.
